analysis.one_liner: Caps annual out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $2,000 per person in marketplace and employer health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2024 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit what people pay out of pocket for prescription drugs in ACA marketplace plans and employer health plans: no more than $2,000 per person or $4,000 per family per year starting in 2026, with the limit rising each year with medical inflation. Today there is an overall out-of-pocket ceiling, but drug costs can consume all of it, leaving patients paying thousands for medications on top of premiums. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it was referred to the Senate health committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with expensive prescriptions — cancer patients, people on insulin, blood thinners, or specialty drugs — who today can hit the plan's full out-of-pocket maximum ($9,450 for an individual in 2025 marketplace plans) just from drug costs. Under the bill, drug cost-sharing alone could never exceed $2,000 per person or $4,000 per family per year, in both marketplace and employer plans. Insurers and employers would absorb the difference, and some of that would likely show up as modestly higher premiums for everyone.

how_it_helps.text: Starting in 2026, no one in an ACA marketplace plan could be required to pay more than $2,000 per year ($4,000 per family) out of pocket for prescription drugs covered by the plan.
The cap rises each year with medical inflation, so the protection does not erode over time.
The same cap would apply to employer group health plans, which cover far more Americans than the ACA marketplaces, by tying employer plan rules to the same standard.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that fund plans would pick up drug costs above the cap; some of that cost would likely be passed back to enrollees as higher premiums.

drawbacks.text: Insurers and employers that fund health plans would bear the added cost when patients stop paying above the cap, and some of that cost would likely be passed back to all enrollees through higher premiums.
The cap covers only cost-sharing on covered drugs; patients can still face large bills for non-covered drugs, specialty pharmacy arrangements, and other out-of-pocket medical costs.
The $2,000 cap is per individual with a $4,000 family cap, so households with several members on expensive medications could still owe $4,000 a year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — protecting seriously ill patients from thousands of dollars in yearly drug bills — is real and large for the roughly one in ten enrollees who hit today's limits. The main drawback is cost: insurers and employers would pay more, and some of that would likely return to consumers as higher premiums or reduced wage growth. The bill offered no offsetting mechanism, which is presumably why it stalled after a one-page referral. Still, the outcome — no vote at all — left the original problem fully intact.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey introduced the Capping Prescription Costs Act of 2024 on July 11, 2024.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on July 11, 2024 — its only action besides introduction.
No further action was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Ten Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one had to absorb the cost of the cap — health insurers and employer health plans keep the status quo — while patients with high drug costs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employer plans; status quo held

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored the $2,000 individual / $4,000 family drug cost-sharing cap.

for.name: 10 Democratic senators (Warnock, Klobuchar, Fetterman, Gillibrand, Blumenthal, Van Hollen, Heinrich, Baldwin, Welch)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all ten were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor schedule in 2024 and did not bring the bill up; with no Republican cosponsors, it had no path to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, so the bill never had the bipartisan support typically needed to move in the Senate.

industries.note: Insurers would have to absorb drug cost-sharing above $2,000 per person per year instead of passing it to patients, which raises their costs; most would respond through premiums or benefit design. The bill does not change insurers' underlying role as the channel for coverage.
Employer plans are covered by the same cap, so self-insured employers would pick up more of their workers' prescription drug costs. The bill died, so no change occurred.

When patients stop paying above a cap, insurers and employers pick up the rest, which can support demand for high-priced drugs. The bill did not include drug price controls, so manufacturers' pricing power is untouched.
